Research

I study how automated systems score speech: where they agree with human raters, where they do not, and who is affected when they get it wrong.

The question has three parts in my work. One is technical: what an automated scorer responds to in a recording, and how far its scores can be trusted. One is about policy: which multilingual students get recognized, and which ones drop out of public data. The newest asks how students and universities judge the use of generative AI.

Scoring Spoken English

Dissertation: validity and fairness of automated speaking assessment

2025 to Present

Examines agreement and decision risk between human holistic ratings and automated scores from the released Speak & Improve Challenge 2025 baseline scorer (Cambridge Speak & Improve Corpus 2025), and what predicts their disagreement. Decision risk here means responses where the human and the automated score land on opposite sides of a cut score, so the same answer would pass with one scorer and fail with the other.

What a first language leaves in L2 speech

2025 to Present

Before a scorer can be judged, it helps to know what in the signal carries a speaker’s first language. Using Speech Accent Archive recordings of Mandarin and English first-language speakers, I describe their English with MFCCs, test which coefficients separate the two groups, and show that a random forest built on that small set classifies better than one built on all thirteen. A companion study uses forced alignment to locate pauses in the same read passage: both groups pause at punctuation about equally, but the Mandarin group pauses far more often where the text gives no punctuation cue.

Multilingual Learners and Policy

The Seal of Biliteracy: access, fidelity and recognition

2025 to Present

How the Seal of Biliteracy is implemented, who can earn it, how students qualify, and whether colleges and employers recognize it. With CEOP colleagues I am also studying Seal attainment by English learner status and district locale across all 50 states and DC; data collection began in 2026. With four colleagues I reviewed fifteen years of research on the Seal for TESOL Quarterly, asking who can reach it, whether programs stay true to its purpose, and what it is worth to students afterward.

I worked on the review in summer 2025 as a graduate research assistant on Project SEMILLA (Supporting Educators, Math Instructors, and Language Learners for Advancement), a $2.44 million project funded by the U.S. Department of Education, Office of English Language Acquisition, at the Center for Educational Opportunity Programs, University of Kansas.

English learners in Kansas public reporting

2026 to Present

How districts report English learner results, which student groups become invisible, and how small cohort sizes create gaps in public data. I conceived and led the study at CEOP in summer 2026. Kansas withholds a subgroup result when fewer than ten students are tested. In our white paper, districts that publish English learner reading results enroll about 98% of the state’s English learners, yet only about 41% of the districts that serve them report: every city district, but only about a quarter of rural ones. Once enrollment is taken into account, the rural gap is no longer statistically significant: small numbers under a uniform threshold, rather than rurality as such, decide who goes unseen. The Kansas analysis is complete (white paper, August 2026; journal version under review), and the study is now extending to about ten more states with CEOP colleagues.

Generative AI and Academic Integrity

With colleagues at Kansas I developed and tested four short instruments for how university students judge the use of generative AI in their coursework, and presented work at AERA on whether campus climate or individual factors better predict academic AI integrity. A manuscript with Hyesun Cho, revised and back under review, looks at raciolinguistic gatekeeping and algorithmic suspicion of Middle Eastern graduate teaching assistants, and I will lead a roundtable on the same topic at TESOL 2027.

Methods

Each method links to the study where I used it.

Measurement

  • Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis of ordinal items (polychoric correlations, parallel analysis, WLSMV)GenAI ethics instruments
  • Reliability: Cronbach’s alpha, McDonald’s omega, Spearman-BrownGenAI ethics instruments
  • Rasch modeling and the linear logistic test model, with a coded Q-matrix of item featuresLLTM study
  • Rater agreement and cut-score decision risk, with bootstrap confidence intervalsdissertation

Statistical modeling

  • Hierarchical regression with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errorsGenAI ethics instruments
  • Crossed random-effects logistic models (lme4); Poisson and negative binomial models for countsacoustic gaps
  • Firth penalized logistic regression for rare and separated outcomesToo Few to Count
  • ANCOVA, MANCOVA and MANOVA with effect sizes, in a pre, post and delayed post-test designaudio-assisted reading
  • Group comparisons with Bonferroni correction, MANOVA and canonical discriminant analysisMFCC framework

Speech and machine learning

  • MFCC feature extraction and random forest classification, compared with McNemar’s testMFCC framework, MFCC pipeline
  • Forced alignment (Montreal Forced Aligner) with acoustic checks in Praat and Parselmouthacoustic gaps
  • Reproducible Python pipelines (librosa, scikit-learn)MFCC pipeline

Corpus and qualitative

  • Corpus analysis with AntConc and WordSmith; chi-square comparisonsbook-review corpus
  • Integrative literature review, reported with PRISMA 2020 itemsSeal of Biliteracy review
